en: May the laurels be eternal
that we knew how to win;
crowned with glory let us live,
or let us swear to die with glory.
Hear, mortals, the sacred cry:
Liberty, liberty, liberty.
Hear the noise of broken chains:
see noble equality on a throne.
There rises on the face of the earth
a new and glorious nation,
its brow crowned with laurels,
and a lion yielded at its feet.
The faces of the new champions
Mars himself seems to animate:
greatness nests in their breasts:
at their march they make all things tremble.
The tombs of the Inca are stirred,
and in their hollows the ardour revives,
seeing renewed by its sons
the ancient splendour of the homeland.
But mountains and walls are felt
to resound with a horrible crash;
the whole country is troubled by cries
of vengeance, of war and of fury.
In the fierce tyrants envy
spat out its pestilent gall;
they raise their bloody standard,
provoking to the cruellest fight.
Do you not see them upon Mexico and Quito
hurl themselves with stubborn rage?
And how, bathed in blood, weep
Potosí, Cochabamba and La Paz?
Do you not see them upon sad Caracas
scatter mourning, weeping and death?
Do you not see them devouring, like wild beasts,
every people they manage to subdue?
Against you, Argentines, dares
the pride of the vile invader:
he already treads your fields, reckoning,
victorious, to trample so many glories.
But the brave, who united swore
to uphold their happy liberty,
to those tigers thirsting for blood
will know how to set strong breasts against them.
The valiant Argentine to arms
runs, burning with spirit and valour:
the bugle of war, like thunder,
resounded in the fields of the South.
Buenos Aires places itself at the head
of the peoples of the illustrious union,
and with robust arms they tear apart
the haughty Iberian lion.
San José, San Lorenzo, Suipacha,
both Piedras, Salta and Tucumán,
La Colonia, and the very walls
of the tyrant in the Banda Oriental,
are eternal inscriptions that say:
here the Argentine arm triumphed;
here the fierce oppressor of the Homeland
bent his proud neck.
Victory covered the Argentine warrior
with its shining wings,
and, dismayed at the sight of him, the tyrant
took to flight in infamy.
His flags, his arms surrender
as trophies to Liberty,
and on wings of glory the people raise
a throne worthy of its great majesty.
From one pole to the other resounds
the sonorous bugle of fame,
and, showing forth the name of America,
it repeats to them: Mortals, hear!...
Now their most worthy throne have opened
the United Provinces of the South;
and the free of the world reply:
To the great Argentine people, hail!
notes: line 2.8: 'rendido' is 'surrendered, subdued, lying vanquished': the lion of Spain at the new nation's feet.

lines 3.7-3.8: 'Lo que ve renovando á sus hijos / De la patria el antiguo esplendor' is loosely constructed; read as 'on seeing the homeland's ancient splendour renewed by its [the Inca's] sons'. It can also be taken as 'which [the ardour] sees its sons renewing'.
lines 6.3-6.4: 'contando ... hollar vencedor' = 'counting on trampling, as victor, so many glories' (the glories of the land).
line 8.2: 'Ambas Piedras': Las Piedras, the battles at two places of that name (Banda Oriental and the Río Piedras).
line 8.4: 'Banda Oriental': the 'Eastern Bank' of the Uruguay river, present-day Uruguay.
